title: Rhoda at the door (Acts 12:1–17)
hook: Peter escapes prison, knocks, and the maid is so happy she forgets to open

segments.voice: Yesterday, Peter and Cornelius, and the old word Gentile. Your line was call no one common. Whose label did you take off? Day eighty-three.

This one starts dark. King Herod, a later Herod than the one in the Christmas story, has James, the brother of John, put to death with the sword. Seeing that it pleases some people, he arrests Peter too, during the Passover week, and plans to bring him out for a public trial when the festival's over. Peter is guarded by four squads of soldiers. The night before the trial he's asleep between two of them, chained to both. And across the city, in a house belonging to a woman named Mary, the mother of John Mark, the church is gathered, praying for him, deep into the night. In the King James Bible: "prayer was made without ceasing of the church unto God for him." Hold on to that. They're praying for exactly this.
screen: `JAMES IS KILLED.` → `PETER IN CHAINS.` → `PRAYER WITHOUT CEASING.`

segments.voice: In the prison, a light. An angel nudges Peter in the side and says, get up, quickly. The chains fall off his wrists. Put on your belt, the angel says, and your sandals. Now your cloak. Follow me. Peter follows, half asleep, sure he's dreaming. Past the first guard, past the second, to the iron gate into the city, which opens by itself. They walk one street, and the angel is gone. And Peter comes to himself in the cool night air and realizes: this is real. So he goes to Mary's house, where they're all praying, and knocks at the outer gate. A servant girl comes to answer. Her name is Rhoda, and it means rose. And here's Luke's line: "And when she knew Peter's voice, she opened not the gate for gladness, but ran in, and told how Peter stood before the gate." She's so happy she forgets to open the door. She runs in to tell everybody. And the room full of people praying for Peter's release says, in the King James: "Thou art mad." She insists. Then it must be his angel, they say. Meanwhile, outside, a wanted man stands in the street: "But Peter continued knocking." When they finally open it, they're astonished. Notice two things. First, Luke gives the servant girl a name. In a story full of kings, soldiers and apostles, the one who recognizes the voice is Rhoda, and she's remembered. Second, the church prayed hard, and when the answer came, it was standing on the doorstep, and they almost didn't let it in.
screen: `CHAINS FALL. FOLLOW ME.` · `SHE OPENED NOT THE GATE FOR GLADNESS.` · `THOU ART MAD.` · `BUT PETER CONTINUED KNOCKING.` · then, large: `ANSWERED PRAYERS KNOCK TOO.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: laugh at one good surprise. Sit, and breathe. Think back over the last month or so for something good that arrived, that you'd hoped for, and then nearly missed, or didn't believe at first. A message you left unread. Good news you second-guessed. Someone's kindness you assumed must be a mistake. Let yourself smile at it, or laugh, the way you'd laugh at Rhoda running in with the door still shut. If you pray, you can say thank you. The bell holds the time.
Rhoda at the door. A servant girl so glad she forgot to open it, and a room that called her mad.

Your line: answered prayers knock too. Today, open the door to one good thing you've been treating as too good to be true. Tomorrow, a purple-cloth merchant, and singing at midnight. Day eighty-three.

howItsDone: Christians often tell the story of Rhoda with a smile, as a picture of praying hard and then being surprised by the answer. Catholics and others read Peter's escape on the feast of Saints Peter and Paul, June 29.

fork.reveal: she opened not the gate for gladness, but ran in. the room told her she was mad, and Peter continued knocking.

original.note: Greek: rose. The name of the servant girl who knew Peter's voice.

trapdoor: what you thought: a funny little scene with a maid.
what it means: the church prays all night for Peter's release, and when he's knocking at the door, they don't believe it.
what a scholar hears: Luke names a servant girl, Rhode, in a story of kings; the house belongs to Mary, mother of John Mark, a home where, Acts says, many were gathered praying.

notes: Herod here is Herod Agrippa I, grandson of Herod the Great; stated as 'a grandson of the Herod from the Christmas story'. Confirm.
Acts 12:1–11 is the first reading at the Mass of the day for Saints Peter and Paul (June 29) in the Roman lectionary; confirm, and confirm other churches that read it then.
'Passover week' renders 'the days of unleavened bread' (12:3–4). Confirm.
The script calls the author of Acts 'Luke', following church tradition; many scholars treat the authorship as uncertain. Confirm the traditional name is acceptable without a qualifier.

Review (days 76–93 editor pass, 2026-10-01): cut the superlative 'one of the most human [lines] in the Bible'; the genealogy (Agrippa I as grandson of Herod the Great) is no longer stated, only that this is a later Herod; 'up all night' softened to match Acts 12:6, 12; trapdoor no longer counts 'one of the few homes ... named in Acts'.
